utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As today is Thursday, I seem to have no schedule for next week, no timetable. And I think it's high time that I got one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. You should have had one, because we got one yesterday, and you should have had it too. Mr. Nice, what are we on? I think the 5th of September schedule? Well, it's one that I've got.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. It's just been handed over now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Oh, there's another one coming up which is the 9th. I'm sorry, I'm behind too. Yes. Make sure the accused has it. Yes, we'll -- let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. If you'd like to sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And could you remember, please, both of you - this is the witness, counsel, and the accused - to leave a pause between the questions and answers. It's most important from the point of view of security and also from the point of view of the interpreters being able to interpret. So wait till the other speaker is finished before speaking yourself. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, there is a sheet of paper in front of you. On the sheet, is that your name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you testify in the trial of Mr. Dokmanovic under the pseudonym Q?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution would like to tender the transcript of the testimony and the exhibits used during the testimony. And tab 2 is actually the name sheet used in the Dokmanovic case that was just shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 535.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I will now summarise the evidence given during the Dokmanovic trial and just with a few additional questions. The witness is of Serb ethnicity. In 1991, he lived in Serbia. Towards the end of August or beginning of September 1991, the witness heard appeals for men to join the Serb forces for the battle in Vukovar. He was aware that volunteers could either join the JNA or enlist in special recruitment offices.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, I have a few additional questions: At that time, did you hear any accounts in the media related to the Serb civilians in Vukovar and what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Well, they did say on television that they were being persecuted.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what media? That television, do you know which station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you exactly - I can't remember - but I watched television in Novi Sad, and they were all Serbian television stations.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you believe the accounts that you heard on TV?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did these accounts influence your decision to volunteer to the Serb forces in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you later on find that these reports were true, these accounts of persecution?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Well, mostly the reports were exaggerated and weren't actually quite true.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I'll continue now with the summary. Witness C-007 went to the volunteers enlistment office. From there, he was sent to Sid, where he was told to report to the TO command. The TO command was generally referred to as ministry, with a certain Bogunovic being the minister and belonging to the Goran Hadzic government. The security command received directions from the JNA security officer Petkovic. The witness was issued uniform and weapons. At the TO headquarter in Sid, he observed Major Kavalic from the Guards Brigade attending a meeting. The witness attended training exercises with the Guards Brigade and was subsequently transferred with the Guards Brigade to Negoslavci, where the JNA headquarters was located. From there, he took part in military actions in Vukovar from end of September 1991 onwards. While in the JNA headquarters in Vukovar -- in Negoslavci, the witness had to sign a document that enabled him to receive a salary and compensation. Stories were spread among the conscripts about atrocities perpetrated by the Croatian side. This caused an incredible phobic atmosphere among the young conscripts. The stories enraged the young soldiers and made them fearful at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I have two additional questions, sir. While you were in the Guards Brigade in Negoslavci and later on in actions in Vukovar, did you and your unit receive your orders from JNA officers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes, I did receive orders from JNA officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: During the fighting, did you make any observations as to the weaponry of the Croat forces in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Well, the Croatian forces predominantly had hunting weapons. As to artillery weapons, I think they had mortars -- 82-millimetre mortars. That was the highest calibre they had.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in relation to an operation in the Blaz Jovanovic complex, were you told anything about the number of the Croat soldiers that were opposing you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: We were told that opposite us were strong Croatian forces, between 300 and 400 men, which wasn't true. There might have been some 20 soldiers, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I'll continue with the summary. Sometime in October 1991, the witness joined the TO of Vukovar. The commander of the Vukovar TO was Miroljub Vujovic. The TO headquarter was located in an area of Vukovar called Petrova Gora. The Velepromet warehouse was at the old logistic base.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, just one question: Was there also a JNA post or headquarters in Petrova Gora?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Well, there was a sort of command there, headquarters. I don't know what kind exactly. I didn't have any contacts with it. And there was some major there, but I can't remember his surname exactly now either.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness TO unit got several assignments to clear certain areas, meaning to go from house to house and remove the people in them. The witness took part in those cleansing operations in Vukovar, among others in the neighbourhood named Supoderica.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, to clarify a matter from the transcript, did you -- did anyone train you how to go about the task of clearing a house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Well, I did have a short period of training before I came to Negoslavci, that was in Sid, and it lasted for two to three days. And I was given the necessary instructions there as to how to enter cellars, how to search houses. Things of that kind, how that job was done. And then later on an officer whom I knew, because he was from Borovo - I knew him from before - he explained how we were to establish whether there were any children in the cellar and things of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Those civilians taken out of the houses, where were they taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: The civilians were taken to Velepromet, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I'll continue with the summary. Several incidents occurred during such cleansing operations. In one incident, a Montenegrin volunteer named Cetinje was shot at by a man with long blond hair. As a result, Cetinje killed all Croats with long blond hair that they came across. In addition, Cetinje also killed people with the surname Barisic due to a historical event. Another TO member with the name Kizo, nickname, bragged that he and Cetinje were at Velepromet executing civilians. TO commanders held regular meetings at the house of Stanko Vujanovic, who was also in a superior position. Among those people attending the meetings was a JNA captain by the name of Radic. The witness believes that he was actually staying in the house. The meetings were often held in the evening before an action. Vujanovic's house was also used as a warehouse for supplies, such as weapons and ammunition. The witness understood Captain Radic's role to be a coordinator between the TO units fighting on the left wing and the other units. The TO cooperated with the JNA. General plans were made by the JNA, who also supplied the TO with ammunition and weapons. The TO units got assignments from the JNA but had a certain discretion how to go about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, one additional question: Was there a soldier with the name of Stuka living in Vujanovic's house? And if so, how was he related, if at all, to Captain Radic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: The soldier nicknamed Stuka was living in Vujanovic's house, and he was a direct soldier of Captain Radic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This person, did he have a reputation of killing people, and did you actually observe him doing that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see him directly killing anybody, but I did see when he tried or, rather, when he went to throw a bomb into a WC, where there were two members of Jehovah's Witnesses. Now, whether he actually killed them or not, I don't know. Could you just repeat the first part of your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The first part was: Did he have a reputation of killing people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes, he did have the reputation of a pathological killer.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you come across a group of SRS volunteers that participated in the military actions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean by "SRS." What is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where were they staying, and who was their leader?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Their leader was Kameni, and, well, there were quite a lot of them. I think that when they arrived in Vukovar, there could have been some 100 or 140 of them, I'm not quite sure of the number. But they were stationed in the same street where Kameni and Stanko Vujanovic had their houses. I'm not sure of those streets' name now. But as there were a lot of them, I assume they were accommodated in the houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were they part of the TO in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Well, I can't quite be sure as to whether officially they did come under the command of the Territorial Defence, but they did take part in the war together with the Territorial Defence, so it would appear that they were part -- it appeared that they were part of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did Vojislav Seselj visit them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: I saw him visit them once. Possibly he might have done so on some other occasion as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I'll continue now with the summary. TO members were involved in looting, as was the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In relation to the looting and involvement of the JNA, did you make any observation to this effect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Well, the reason I left the JNA unit was because I reported that some soldiers -- let me put it this way -- took from a house, my friend's house, some jewellery they found there. So I reported this, and the jewellery was subsequently returned, but that was one of the reasons for which I had to leave that unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in relation to the looting, did you see any -- any shipments to certain officers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: I was told once when I was a member of the Guards Unit that we should help load up some boxes full of technical equipment, and the boxes had the names and addresses of some officers on them who lived in Belgrade. But I don't know what happened to them afterwards -- with them afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I'll continue with the summary. On the 19th of November, the witness went to the Vukovar hospital. The fighting had stopped either on the 17th or the 18th of November. The witness saw JNA military police at the gate. He also saw TO members on the premises. The witness saw Veselin Sljivancanin in the hospital courtyard. The witness had previously encountered him twice during the military operations in Vukovar. Within the hospital, he saw a group including Stanko Vujanovic, several TO members, and one of them threatened to shoot Dr. Bosanac. Terrible stories were going around about her, so that the TO member wanted to shoot her on the spot. On the 20th of November, the witness was told that Vujanovic men had snatched a group of Ustashas from the JNA soldiers. The witness, together with several others, went to Ovcara. When they arrived at Ovcara, he observed buses full of people parked close to the hangar. He went into the hangar, where he saw several Serbs, among them Miroljub Vujovic, his deputy Djankovic, Stuka, and several TO members. He did not notice any soldiers in or outside the hangar. The soldiers at Vukovar formed two parallel lines and forced the detainees to pass the gauntlet. The soldiers would severely beat the detainees, using all kinds of objects, and also kick them. He also realised that they were the people -- the detainees were the people from the Vukovar hospital. The witness saw at one point in time a high-ranking JNA officer, probably a colonel, accompanied by another JNA soldier. The JNA officer tried to talk the TO members out of beating the prisoners, but the soldiers refused to stop. The JNA officer then left. No JNA intervention followed. Your Honours, I would now like to go into private session to continue the summary, because it's now related to matters that may reveal the identity of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: While at Ovcara, the witness observed that Miroljub Vujovic, the TO commander, was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned during your testimony that huge harvesters were working when you returned to Ovcara. Why was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether the interpretation was correct. They were combine harvesters.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And do you know why they were working?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Well, they were leaned -- leaning up against the outside gates. As the hangar is a metal one, they were working to make -- create noise in the hangar, to prevent the noises from the execution shots from being heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you were outside the hangar, could you actually hear the shots?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Of course. When I was in front of the hangar, you could hear the shooting.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And inside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Inside the hangar, you couldn't hear a thing, just the noise of the engines working.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was there an incident that someone actually shot within the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: As far as I know, nobody was killed in the hangar. Just at one point there was shooting in order to instil fear, and Miroljub Vujovic reacted and issued a warning. It was Djankovic who did this and he was told not to do that any more and to frighten -- not to frighten the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What were the detainees told when the selection started?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: They were told that they would be questioned. And that they would see what would happen to them next, that -- they were just told that they would be questioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I'll continue with the summary. Inside the hangar, the detainees were selected into small groups of about ten who were taken away to the execution place and shot. At one point during the executions, the soldiers ran out of ammunition. Miroljub Vujovic told everyone that he went to the JNA to ask for more ammunition. The execution lasted until after midnight. The witness did not know how many detainees were killed, but had heard the figure of 372 detainees being at Ovcara. Your Honours, we would now, for the last question -- for the last section, go back into private session, because it's again something related to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. C-007, you gave your statement to the investigators between the 9th and 15th of December, 1997.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes, around those dates. I don't remember the exact dates, but probably that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where was this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: In the barracks. I think UNPROFOR was securing the barracks in Vukovar at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In the meantime, since you gave that statement and before coming to The Hague, did you see the investigators or meet with the investigators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't hear the beginning of the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You gave your statement in December 1997.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it says on the statement, so that's not at issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But since that time, since December 1997, up until your arrival here in The Hague, did you have any contacts or meetings with the investigators to whom you gave that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: I think I did. I can't say for sure, because I made that statement, and when I was making that statement, I didn't want to be a witness. But later on I changed my opinion. So I had to contact the investigator to tell him that I'd changed my mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how many contacts did you have with the investigator from the time you gave your statement until you arrived in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: I really don't remember. One or two? I don't know. All this was between December 1997 and up until, I think, June 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You say that with your son-in-law or brother-in-law - I won't mention his name, as I have to protect your identity - in September 1991 as a volunteer you reported to the TO command in Sid. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: First we reported to Kraljevica and Marka in Novi Sad, and from there we were sent to Sid.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You did this in order to be able to choose where you would go; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes. If I had reported to the barracks directly, they would have probably sent me to Banja.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I don't know where they would probably have sent you, but you reported in order to go to Vukovar specifically.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And that is the wish you expressed when you got there, I assume, as a volunteer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And then as a volunteer you were assigned as a guard in the TO staff; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Then in the third paragraph on page 4, you say that a couple of days later you were sent for additional training with a part of the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The commander of which was a certain major - I won't mention his name so that we won't have to go into private session. Now, tell me, where was this training provided?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: It was a rather large house outside Sid. How far from the town itself, I really don't know because I went in a vehicle. So I don't know. Anyway, it was close to Sid.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Now tell me, please, you claim on page 4 of your statement, paragraph 4 - I assume you have the statement in front of you - that the training was interrupted on the 27th of September, 1991. Allegedly Colonel Mrksic at the time had carried out a coup in Belgrade, arrested about 30 generals and as many politicians. That is what is stated in your statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And according to information that you give, a military police battalion took over the headquarters building in Belgrade, et cetera. That is what it says in your statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes. I don't see what is in dispute there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Well, how could you talk of such nonsense? What kind of military coup was carried out? Who were the generals and politicians arrested by Mrksic? What happened in Belgrade? You are telling us this in your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One at a time. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you. I'm saying what the soldiers told me when they returned they had done. Of course, I wasn't present, so I can't say that this happened 100 per cent. I think it says somewhere that I was told this by soldiers. Training was interrupted. They went to Belgrade. And they returned a day or two later and told me what they had done. Maybe they arrested you too. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. 007, surely the public would have known that Colonel Mrksic had staged a coup and arrested 30 generals and as many politicians. If the other information is equally reliable that you're providing, what am I going to ask you? Are you speaking seriously about this coup?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is a comment by you and irrelevant. What the witness says is this is what he was told about, whether it happened or not. Yes. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But you don't know who those generals and politicians were that were arrested, according to what you said in the statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: You mean their names?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: No. Thirty of them and as many politicians.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Very well. You say in paragraph 5 that a couple of days later you received orders to move to Vukovar. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And who gave you those orders to move to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: My superior.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you were part of one of the units of the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: I was the 1st Company of the 1st Battalion of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Very well. And on the way there, you joined the rest of the Guards Unit, so you were part of the Guards Unit; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And where did you join the rest of the Guards Unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Well, where I was having training, there was the military police company. I really don't know. Somewhere near Sid. I can't tell you exactly. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you claim that you were put up in Negoslavci in the house of a friend of yours whose name I will not read out so that it may not be linked to you as you are a protected witness. So you were accommodated in the house of a friend of yours in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: When you asked me where I joined the Guards Brigade, did you mean while I was in Sid attending training? This part of the unit that was separate from the Guards Brigade, this battalion of military police, joined the brigade as it was going towards Negoslavci, so I don't know exactly whether it was in Sid, before Sid, or after Sid.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But you say that you were accommodated in the house of your friend in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes, when we arrived in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How could you as a soldier of a Guards Brigade go to stay in a friend's house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: That is not what it says in my statement. We were first put up in some houses. And as the houses were in very bad shape, I asked the officer - I think he was a lieutenant - whether I could find some better accommodation, and the whole squad was put up in the house of this friend of mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So with permission of your superior officer, you were put up in your friend's house.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Not just me but the whole squad.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Some ten or so of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let us leave out the details linked to this. Tell me, how much time in all did you spend as a member of the Guards Unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: You mean the battalion of the military police in the Guards?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, in the Guards. I'm not specifying whether it was a military police battalion or some other unit. I'm just asking how much time you spent in the Guards Unit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: The point is that, as far as I know, the TO was also under the command of the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But that's the TO. I'm asking you, because you say that you were a member of the Guards Unit. At what point in time? When did you stop being a member of the Guards Unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but around the 20th of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So already the 20th of October you were no longer a member of the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: I can't tell you the exact date, but around that date. Maybe a day before or a day later.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: On page 5, paragraph 4, you say that you spent some time in front of the barracks in Vukovar, where next to you there were two tanks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That the crews were made up of young soldiers, conscripts, and the inhabitants of Vukovar came up to you quite freely, asking where they were from and talking to you. There were no incidents, were there??

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: I don't know whether the inhabitants were talking to these people with the tanks, but I do know -- I don't remember saying that they talked to those soldiers on the tanks. But if they had asked them anything, they would have given answers. There would have been no problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In front of the JNA barracks, there were two tanks. "The crews were made up of conscripts without much combat experience. Some of them were even sitting on their tanks reading comic books."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: "To complete the picture, people from the neighbouring houses were coming out and asking us who we were, because, as they said, they had never seen soldiers like us."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: They were asking us, not the tank crews, as they belonged to another unit. I think that was the Mitrovica Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So the tank crews were regular soldiers and you were already in the TO.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: No. I was still in the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I see, you were in the Guards Brigade. So this was still in October?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes, this was the beginning of October. 1st, 2nd, or 3rd, I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In the fifth paragraph on page 5, you say that you saw some JNA tanks moving towards the centre of town and you thought then, as you say here, that they must have fired at Croats.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: I don't remember that passage from my statement, because it was translated into English and then back from the English into Serbian, but I can tell you what it was all about. The tanks were moving towards the centre, and we went alongside as security for the tanks, and the tanks speeded up, if I can put it that way, left us, went towards the centre, fired a couple of shells, and came back. So I'm not sure about the translation. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Well, I thought that that was a bit strange and not very logical. Anyway, did you hear the tanks open fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what were they firing at?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What has been handed to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's the English version of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't know if that's going to be much use.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But let the witness have that, if it's of any use to him. Yes, let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You say in that same paragraph, "After the tanks withdrew towards Negoslavci, the Croats started shelling us." That's what it says. That's how it reads.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And then you go on to say, "Later on I learnt that the shelling was only a part of the morning routine."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So they shelled you all the time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, that particular morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And then you go on to say -- you say that, "It was part of the usual morning routine and despite that, two sergeants, a lieutenant and a captain - I do not remember their names - were wounded in the shelling, so that we were practically left without officers."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: "The wounded were taken care of, and we then moved inside the barracks."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: What did you say? I don't know about this bit of going into the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It says, "The wounded were taken care of, and we then moved inside the barracks." I'm reading this from your statement, actually.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes. This is how it was. A number of unit members went inside the barracks. I myself stayed outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Tell me this, then, please: As you say at the end of that paragraph on page 5 that you returned and that there was a skirmish with the TO members, a short skirmish.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was the reason for the skirmish with the members of the TO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Well, we didn't know that they were members of the Territorial Defence. And as we were wearing camouflage uniforms, they thought we were the Zengas, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So there was a misunderstanding; is that it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And then in page 3 -- page 6, paragraph 3, you say you heard rumours going round as to what was happening to the members of the JNA in Vukovar allegedly, that you considered them to be impossible, and construed in order to create an atmosphere and phobias, you say, among the young recruits which were to be brought into a position to kill elderly people, children, and anybody else they came across. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Well, I think I said something similar, because that was the effect that was -- on the soldiers. That was how it affected the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who produced that effect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember exactly now which of the officers told us that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you read the statement by your father, do you think that it would have had that effect on the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: I have not read my father's statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this, then: You say that they could shoot old women and even children. During the time you allegedly spent within the Guards Unit, did you see any soldier or JNA officer kill anybody, for that matter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: I didn't see them killing women and children.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Well, did you see a soldier or a JNA officer kill anybody at all? Did you personally see a soldier or a JNA officer kill anybody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's fine. Very well. Now we can move on. You claim that you heard that a major who was in command - and I won't state his name, because you say he was your commander, commanding officer - after the death of a younger soldier --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. There's a mistake here. He was a young sergeant, was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And he was very close to him, fond of him. He went to a cellar in Negoslavci and killed two prisoners there. That's what you say in paragraph 5 of page 6.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: I also say that that's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: All right. So you're inclined to believe the story, are you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: I have believed in many things during my life.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: All right. But you are inclined to believe that story; whereas, the killing of the soldier -- so you're inclined to believe in this story but you're not inclined to believe in the story of the killings of soldiers, and you consider that they were created to instil phobia among the population.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what you mean. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Apparently there's a set of headphones which are creating a problem. Have we got them? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Very well. At all events, this was an event that you heard about; is that it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You personally know nothing about it, that this major killed anybody, in fact.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: All right. Very well. A moment ago, during the examination-in-chief, you said that the members of the Croatian National Guard Corps and the police, that is to say, the Croatian forces, for the most part had had hunting weapons. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And a moment ago you say that they shelled you and carried out routine morning shellings. So how were they able to shell you? What weapons did they use? Surely not hunting rifles.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: No. They used an 82-millimetre mortar to shell us.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Well, tell us, then: Do you think that all the fighting there would have gone on for as long as three months had these people really only just had these hunting rifles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Well, I'm personally convinced that you -- had you appointed a more intelligent general, it would have all gone on for just six or seven hours or two or three days, not longer than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't in a position to appoint generals of that kind.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: But you did appoint a general to lead everybody later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's what you think. In paragraph 2, page 7, you say that members of the Territorial Defence liberated parts of the town and they were called Ivo Andric and Blaz Jovanovic, and you say that later on you, as members of the JNA, went over there yourselves. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You left the JNA after, as was emphasised by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, some looting carried out by a soldier.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So what was it in actual fact? I understood it that some jewellery was stolen from a house, that he stole some jewellery from somebody's house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Well, the settlement was empty, and the soldiers when searching the houses found some jewellery. And of course, it would have been military procedure for them to have handed over the jewellery to an officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Anyway, there was this jewellery theft, which you reported.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The result of you having reported the theft was that they found the soldier, the jewellery confiscated and returned to its rightful owner; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So was logical military and civilian procedure conducted, that is to say, that the stolen jewellery was found straight away and returned to its rightful owner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: In that particular case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So what, then, was the reason for your departure from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: After that, the soldiers were hostile towards me, and they claimed that they would set fire to the houses and that it wasn't worth losing one's life for other people's houses. The frontline was situated opposite my own house at the time, and it was logical that they would set fire to my house, so that is why I -- there was this argument between me and the army, and the sergeant said that I should go and speak to the major. And after that interview -- and it says here in the statement that he advised me to move to the Territorial Defence, which was a valid piece of advice.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did anybody set fire to your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Five times.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Well, unofficially it was burnt by the Ustashas and three times by --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But it didn't burn down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Could you repeat who it was who burnt the house again. You said three times -- "it was burnt by the Ustashas and three times by --" and we haven't got recorded who the three times it was by.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Twice -- I said twice it was burnt by the Ustashas and three times by the JNA army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: All right. You say that when you came to that settlement, the Blaz Jovanovic complex, in fact, that you were still in the JNA, weren't you, at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And then you say that you met Major Sljivancanin for the first time then and there. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: The first time during the war I meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: All right. And those parts of town were not taken control of by the JNA, were they, nor were any pretensions made towards it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: I already said that. First of all, those parts of town were won over by the Territorial Defence, then they were occupied by the JNA, because the Territorial Defence didn't have enough soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So it did place those areas under its control, but the JNA did not actually take control of it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you say that in the Blaz Jovanovic complex you stayed there for some -- about ten days and that it was very unpleasant because you were constantly subjected to Croatian gunfire; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: I don't see where it says that in my statement. Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Maybe I can help. It's the paragraph after you mentioned Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which page are we on?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's on page 7, second paragraph, and it's after the paragraph where Major Sljivancanin is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Very well. You say, "We stayed in the Blaz Jovanovic complex for about ten days, holding our positions against, as we were told, 300 to 400 Ustashas, who were across the street. To be honest --"

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: "To be honest, I did not believe that number. We were not comfortable there, as we were exposed to constant fire. Sometimes even from the JNA positions." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That means that you were subjected to fire from the Croatian side and from the JNA as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You were a JNA unit yourselves.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Exactly so.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was anybody killed at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: A member of the Territorial Defence was hit by a sniper, but he was hit by Croatian sniper fire. That is quite certain. And I think that some shrapnels wounded two or three soldiers, but I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So the one that was killed by -- from the Croatian side was killed by a hunting rifle; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: No, a sniper, 762 millimetre or 7.9 millimetre, one or the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So nobody was killed except that one man killed by the Croats. What do you mean when you say that fell casualty? I mean, was anybody killed? Did the JNA kill anybody there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: We were told every morning that there would be artillery preparation for an attack, so every morning, from the Blaz Jovanovic complex, we were transferred to the Ivo Andric complex. And once the artillery preparations were through, we would go back to the Blaz Jovanovic complex position. After an hour or two, we would be told again that there was artillery preparation going on or an air attack, so we once again have to withdraw to the Ivo Andric complex and then half an hour, an hour later, we went back to Blaz Jovanovic. And this would happen five or six times a day.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So that was your drill. All right. I don't want to go into that, but let's go back to the jewellery. Can you tell us the name of the man who stole the jewellery? Because you reported him, and you must have known his name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there really any significance in that? What possible significance is there in it? And if there is any significance, we'll go into private session. Can you remember the name, Witness C-007? If so, we'll go to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember the name. But Mr. Milosevic can check it out. It must have been recorded in the army records, the Guards Brigade, that looting had taken place, because the jewellery was returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I can see that you have explained to us that there was an investigation, that the jewellery was confiscated and returned, and the man probably arrested.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: I don't know what happened to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But as you left the JNA - and we've cleared that point up, that that was in October -

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: About the 20th of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Right. That means one month, a whole month before the fall of Vukovar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So why did you stay on in Vukovar at all in the first place, in view of the fact that you had left the JNA? Why did you stay in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: I didn't leave the JNA. I left the Guards Brigade. I was just transferred from one unit to another, to the Territorial Defence in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So you moved from the JNA to the Territorial Defence; is that it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, the TO and the Guards Brigade were also under the guard of Mrksic, or rather, the Territorial Defence was under the command of the Territorial Brigade. That whole sector was under the command of the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: All right. When you moved into the Territorial Defence, you were under the immediate command of the commander of the Territorial Defence. I don't know whether we mentioned his name in open session or not, so we don't have to mention it, I don't suppose. I think it was mentioned in open session, however; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll check that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, there shouldn't be a problem with that. Yes, it's no problem.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So the command of the Territorial Defence, you say, was Miroljub Vujovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in paragraph 3, page 9 you say that you happened to wound yourself by accident when you were a TO member. How did that come about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: You mean the exact date?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you when that happened.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date, but it must have been recorded because I was hospitalised in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, how long were you out -- away from the unit of the Territorial Defence due to your injuries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Five or six hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Only five or six hours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes. I shot myself in my big toe from an automatic rifle. It wasn't a serious injury.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. There's no need then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. And it's pointed out that it's -- it's half past, although, that clock is a bit fast. We'll adjourn now. Mr. Milosevic, we've considered how long you should have for the witness. We've considered time which has -- some of which has been wasted already. You've had very nearly one hour. But we'll give you another half an hour to finish this cross-examination. Witness C-007, could you bear in mind not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include the Prosecution team. We'll adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. C-007, is it correct that individuals came to Vukovar in order to have an adventure simply and that's why they enlisted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Partly that is correct, but I think that they enlisted in Sid, not in Vukovar. I don't think that there was a chance for anyone to come to Vukovar of his own free will, as far as the Serb side is concerned, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But volunteers usually do come of their own free will.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Of their own free will.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You believe that nobody came to Vukovar to enlist with the TO there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how anybody could have reached Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: All right. I see. If you don't know about it, I won't ask you more about this. Tell me something else. You say that you saved at least 100 to 300 persons, at least, while you were in Vukovar. Civilians, that is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes. I got them out of a cellar. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How come you cannot mention a single name?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we in -- all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: On page 11 in paragraph 2 of your statement, you say that while you were in Vukovar, every day you spent about 2.500 to 5.000 rounds of ammunition, a day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who did you shoot at?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: The enemy.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: 2.500 to 5.000 rounds a day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: It's not in my statement, but I did this because I tried to secure crossings across the road. And when my unit was supposed to cross the street, then I would shoot at roofs, buildings, anything, so that they would be safe while crossing the street. That's why I used up so much ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Didn't you exaggerate this a bit, I mean, having spent that much ammunition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: I know because I filled the clips, the ammunition clips every day, so I know exactly how much I used up.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, PKT.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Tell me, please, how many people did you kill on that occasion, if you shot 3.000 bullets a day? How many people did you kill?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: For the most part, my shooting was by way of prevention.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You did not shoot at anyone. You were simply shooting at buildings.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: On page 12, in paragraph 2, you stated that a person who has a certain nickname - I don't need to mention that nickname, so that we would not go into closed session - that he bragged to you and he said that at Velepromet he killed 165 people there but that you could not believe him. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you say that you couldn't believe it, he told you to come along with him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But you refused because you were afraid that he would kill someone.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That is probably because you'd feel guilty then.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And do you feel guilty for having participated with a person like that in any kind of activities, if there is such a person who brags about having done things like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: I did not have much choice.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But you did have a choice. You came as a volunteer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Nobody forced you to come and nobody recruited you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: All right. On page 12, in paragraph 3, you say that you were against looting. However, you did a bit of looting yourself, but without the intention of stockpiling things but only for your momentary needs. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So you were looting actually but just a little bit, just a little bit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: I only took things I needed then.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: All right. So that we would not have to go into private session, you said that somebody had given you a cockade.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you have anybody who could confirm that? The person you mention here that gave you a cockade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Well, I cannot remember right now, but I can notify the court within a few days of the exact name and surname of this person.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: All right. If you can, it would be useful. Now, tell me, since you mentioned Major Sljivancanin. You said in your statement that you met Major Sljivancanin at the entrance into the hospital; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And he did not allow you to enter with a weapon; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And he asked that you take off the cockade.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Is it also correct that he told you that inside there were about 300 Croatian soldiers and that you did not want -- and that he did not want you to cause a problem there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in addition to that, he informed you that members of the international community were expected to come there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So he was persistent. He would not allow you to enter without a weapon, and you were supposed to take off your cockade, and you obeyed his orders; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Now, in the hospital, you say that you saw Dr. Njavro and Dr. Bosanac.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Matos too. Perhaps I can expand on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And on this occasion - since this was not in closed session, I'm not going to mention any of the other names that were mentioned in closed session - with a group, there was a certain Stanko Vujanovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And they managed to smuggle themselves into the hospital.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Through the back door.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where there was not a guard.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's what I think. I did not see it, but that's what I assume.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And you claim that he then pointed his rifle at Dr. Bosanac, prepared to kill her.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: This is a volunteer who was with him then.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But you reacted quickly, and you saved her life; is that right? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: No. I was walking out with that volunteer. I was getting out of the hospital, and that's where we came across Dr. Bosanac. And she --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Oh, this was outside the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes, at the exit. It's one of those small back doors. I don't know exactly. And then she addressed this third person who was with us and then this volunteer understood that this is Vesna Bosanac, because she had -- what's this thing called? She had her name and surname written on this little plate, and he wanted to kill her.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you prevented that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know that even Vesna Bosanac did not mention in her statement that somebody wanted to kill her?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: I don't know what she mentioned, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course. He can't comment on what she may have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: All right. Tell me --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Can I explain this to you, why she made no comment about this? But it has to be in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go into closed session briefly, since the matter has been raised. Yeah, private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You also say, generally speaking, that the TO had taken certain locations, certain sites, certain neighbourhoods, and then afterwards the JNA would come in and take control over these places. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes, especially because at first the Territorial Defence did not have sufficient manpower to keep everything under their own control.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That practically means that the JNA was only securing the area.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: All right. Is it correct that members of the TO in barracks kidnapped a number of prisoners from the JNA, members of the National Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: As far as I know, rumour had it that they kidnapped about 300 to 400 people who were taken from the hospital to the barracks. Now, where they actually abducted them is something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Is it correct that this was done by threatening the officers and soldiers who were present there with weapons, threatening to kill them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: I was not in that group, but that was the story.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: All right. After that, you went to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How much time did you spend in Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Approximately about eight hours, approximately. I really cannot remember now exactly how much time. And I don't know exactly when everything was over at Ovcara, so it was, say, between six to eight hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, since a short while ago in the examination-in-chief you gave a description and you say that some members of the TO beat these prisoners who were members of the National Guards Corps and of the Croatian police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And then some JNA officer intervened with a commander and protested why they were beating prisoners.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Oh, no. People were lined up. So then when these members of the ZNG and the MUP, when they got off the buses, they went through lines of people. And they addressed this man as colonel. I'm not sure. I didn't see his insignia. And he tried to stop this so they would not have to run a gauntlet. And the man realised that he couldn't do anything and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I wrote this down. You said that this JNA officer tried to persuade the Territorial Defence members not to beat the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So he tried to prevent the beating. But while he was there, they tried -- they beat them and he tried to stop hit. But while he was there, there was no killing. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: At that moment, when that colonel was there, there was no killing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But he was trying to prevent the beating of prisoners; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And later on, when you say that people were killed, it was my understanding on the basis of what you were saying that at that time there was no one there from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: What do you mean "there"?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By the hangar and around the hangar, within a two to three hundred metre diameter there wasn't anyone, but say 500 metres away, there was a small yellow house where there were a few soldiers. Quartermasters -- I'm not sure. But there was a small unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: All right. A couple of hundred metres away there was a small yellow house and there was a group of people belonging to quartermasters, logistics.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: I don't know exactly which group they belonged to and which arms and services they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: At any rate, at Ovcara or near Ovcara there wasn't anyone when these people were killed. I mean, there was no one from the JNA there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: I didn't see anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, do you know who was in command when all those events were taking place at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: The only commander present there, as far as I know, was Miroljub. And he behaved as if he was the commander or the organiser of all this. I don't know how to put it. He was obeyed over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This Miroljub from Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he an official in the TO of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: He was the commander of the TO. At least, that is how he introduced himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You say that some combine harvesters were making a noise.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Outside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This couldn't have attracted anyone's attention.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The noise was made so that the shots could not be heard.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes. But the shots could not be heard in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were the harvesters in the hangar or outside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: They were outside the hangar, leaning on the hangar walls.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Just a moment for me to see whether I have time for a few more questions. You said something about things being taken away. You mentioned an incident when you loaded onto trucks cardboard boxes with the addresses of officers on them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: The addresses -- yes, the addresses were in Belgrade, private addresses.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Private addresses. I see. Well, do you know that in those days various officers were evacuating their families or moving out after the fall of Vukovar and were sending their belongings? Why are you attributing this to looting? Do you know for certain that things were looted, that that was loot, or was it the property of those officers who were sending their belongings in cardboard boxes to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: I don't know what to say in answer to that, but I don't know that officers had lived in that area before. This was in the Ivo Andric area of town.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But you do not have any information as to the contents of those boxes and especially not that they contained loot.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Maybe one could check whether officers were living in part of town. I don't know. I can't guarantee that, but...

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: On what grounds did you come to that allegation that officers were sending stolen goods to their home addresses? Why couldn't it be officers sending their own things?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: It was logical because all the officers present there were from Belgrade, and things were being sent to Belgrade addresses.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So they were sending them to their own address.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes, those officers over there were inhabitants --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Inhabitants of what town? They're JNA officers. They're sending goods to their addresses. I'm asking you how did you come to make that allegation that they were stolen goods and that an officer was stealing things? Apart from this one soldier that you said you saw and that you reported and who was caught and the jewellery returned, the stolen jewellery returned, did you see any other JNA member looting anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: I didn't even see this person actually going from house to house and collecting things. All I saw I said in my statement; that I saw these cardboard boxes loaded into a truck in an area which had been liberated a day or two prior to that. Just as what I am saying what I am saying, you are saying that this was the property of officers who may have been living there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I can't claim anything in that connection, because I wasn't there. I'm just asking you on what ground did you assume that this was something that had been stolen or looted when you don't have any knowledge, you didn't see any officer stealing or looting or doing anything like that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: I don't know what I could say in answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I see that you don't know what to say. But tell me, as I asked you that already, you didn't see a single officer or JNA member looting anything except for this one who stole jewellery and you reported?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've been over this a great many times. Yes. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it will really be very difficult for me, because the statement is a lengthy one given by this witness to the investigators, and there are several things in connection with which I would like to ask him to clarify for you. I see that he doesn't have his statement in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have your statement, the statement you gave to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at page 13. In the English version, it is page 12, last paragraph. You already said during your examination-in-chief here, answering questions by Mrs. Uertz-Retzlaff, but I would like to ask you in connection with this paragraph: You said that you were armed under full combat gear, including a cockade which you received from a certain person, et cetera. "I was armed and in full combat gear, including the cockade..." Is that right? Page 13.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: The pages are not numbered here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This will be very difficult. Surely the Prosecution has a copy with pages that are numbered. All my pages are numbered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We must try and get on in this way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a copy with the pages numbered in the Serbo-Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think the Prosecution have got one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you said that you were in full combat gear, including the cockade that you had received from a certain person; is that right? But in brackets you said, "I refused to wear the red star of the JNA because for me that was a symbol of communism." Did that person ask you to wear it and you refused it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Then who did you say you didn't want to wear the red star and who made such a request of you to wear it? You said, "To distinguish myself from the communists, whom I could not stand, I wore a cockade."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: When I moved to the TO, I didn't have to wear a star and I had no insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you wear the star while you were in the army? Why did you accept it then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: I had no choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You already said that around the hangar there were no soldiers. At least, you didn't see any. Could you look at page 16, please, where you refer to this officer who was in the hangar. Please find page 16. You stated here that he asked the prisoners not to be beaten. He tried to dissuade them, and they started playing around with him. The people he was standing in front of would stop beating for a moment, but those behind would continue. When he realised what was going on and that some of them even threatened that they would beat him up too, he realised that there was nothing he could do and he left. Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, please look at page 14.
