utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just if you stay there. You are speaking about a superior to him? Given that he's a colonel, who could be his superior, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It depended on the unit he belonged to. I really don't know which unit he belonged to. There were several corps there. There was the Mitrovica Corps. I don't know whether there was the Novi Sad Corps, and there was the Guards Brigade. If he was attached to the Guards Brigade, his superior would be a general. And if he was in the Mitrovica Corps, I don't know who the commander of that corps was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, will you please look at page 14, last paragraph of the B/C/S version. And in the English version, page 14, paragraph 3. In the second sentence, you say that, "Somebody from my group - I don't remember exactly who - told me that he and Vujanovic's people had abducted a group of Ustashas from JNA soldiers." Is that what you said? And what did you mean when you used the term "abducted from the JNA"? You seized them from the JNA? How did they do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Those prisoners or Ustashas had been captured by the JNA, and Vujanovic's men snatched them away from them, took them over.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But "seized them," that sounds as if some sort of force must have been used, for prisoners to be taken from someone in the way that you described. On page 17, you again used this word "seized" or "abducted." Could you explain.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: They were not given them. They were not handed over to them. I was told this, as I stated it here. I didn't ask them to explain how it was possible for them to seize those people from the army, whether they had to fight to do that or not. I just was told this, and I went to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As for the surname Radic, on page 7 of your testimony, page 8, second paragraph of the English version, you spoke of a group that you belonged to. Could you please tell us first, do you realise that it was a paramilitary group or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: What do you mean "paramilitary"?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I mean, in view of the uniforms you wore, the insignia you wore, in view of your position, in view of the fact that those soldiers that you were with had seized the JNA prisoners from the JNA. How did you see yourself? Did you consider yourself to be a member of the TO, or did you consider yourself to be a paramilitary unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: I personally considered myself to be a member of the TO. And at one point we even received some emblems with the coat of arms of the TO of Vukovar, which was -- had been created at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. On that same page 8, you gave the exact names and surnames of these people. And under number 7, I think it is, the name Radic appears, the surname Radic, with the nickname Sarac. This Radic had nothing to do with Captain Radic. And did this Radic have a group of his own?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: No. He was a member of our group.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: He was a member of our group, of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And within which group did the man whom you called Stuka act? In paragraph 1, on page 11 --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Do you want the answer as to whom he officially belonged or whom he was with?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Within which group did he operate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: He was a regular JNA soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know. But when you described on page 10 - and then you went on to -- you continued on page 11 - you said with regard to him that he was a pathological killer and that you only just managed to persuade him not to kill someone. So you were trying to persuade him, dissuade him from killing. So was he a member of your unit; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: He was attached to our unit. Our unit consisted of ten men, two groups of five. Sometimes we would be a group of 15. And he joined us voluntarily because --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So he then was not a member of a unit belonging to the JNA? That's what I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Well, let me see. I can say that then the JNA had no control over him. I think that's putting it correctly. He was officially doing his military service. He was a soldier. As to what he was doing, I think that had nothing to do with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, page 10, when you talk about Radic, in paragraph 3, from the bottom of that page, you said roughly -- no, explicitly, "The command of the TO unit had regular meetings in his house, in Vujanovic's house. I heard, I heard, that one of the persons attending those meetings was a JNA captain by the name of Radic who I believe was also staying in that house." That's what you said. "The meetings were usually held in the evening before an action. I was present at one such meeting, but Captain Radic was not there then." You did not say here at all that Captain Radic -- that you ever saw Captain Radic in that house.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: That's what it says in this statement. But I can add. I did see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But that's what you said earlier on. And in another place, you said that you saw him several times but you didn't say that you saw him there just then.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-007
utterances.text: Let me explain. I would see him in that house, but many people would come to that house, because it was the only one that had electricity. One could watch television there. So it wasn't at all strange for him to be there. It was the only house in which one could lead a normal life.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'd also like to show you what you said with respect to Dokmanovic in your statement, compared to the statement you gave previously to the court. You said as follows: "You asked me whether I have seen Slavko Dokmanovic. Before I continue, let me explain and say that I didn't know Dokmanovic at all, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Take care. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was in private session, the actual --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm afraid these -- we will have to remain in private session because of the events to be discussed. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness C-007, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go, but would you just wait until the blinds are pulled down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Pack, is it for you to call the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'll be calling the next witness. Your Honour, perhaps I could deal with something again before the witness comes in. There are documents relating to this witness which the Prosecution considers should be disclosed under Rule 66. These documents were identified, unfortunately, this week. They are documents provided under Rule 70, and the Prosecution has yet to provide clearance for those -- has yet to obtain clearance for those documents, for their release from the relevant providers. It's intended, therefore, that these documents be disclosed as soon as that authority has been obtained. Should the accused consider that further cross-examination of this witness is required once he's received these documents, then of course we would undertake to recall him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you say Rule 66?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes. They're disclosable under Rule 66. They are -- and provided pursuant to Rule 70.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You mean prior statements?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That's right. Unfortunately, they didn't show up on any of our regular searches that we undertake to carry out for witnesses by their name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. If it's necessary for the witness to come back, he'll have to come back. But we'll hear his evidence now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'll call Mr. B-1414.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was he given a pseudonym?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: He's -- will be giving evidence in open session, Mr. Isak Gasi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, will you give the Court, please, your name.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Gasi, Isak.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, did you testify in an earlier case before this Tribunal in 1996?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, can the transcript of prior testimony and one related exhibit be given a new exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit Number 536.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll read a summary of that prior testimony. The witness gave evidence that he was from Brcko. Before the war, he was a canoeist for the former Yugoslavia, participating at the international level. In 1990, he was a member of the SDA executive committee of the town of Brcko. Towards the end of 1990, the witness recalls the military mobilisation of Serb men in the area of Brcko. He recalls rallies prior to the referendum in 1992, at which Serb leaders spoke. He recalls Karadzic, Krajisnik, Plavsic, and Koljevic being there, and on one occasion a minister from Belgrade for Serbs across the Drina. He himself made public pronouncements on television; he said that they should try to live together in Bosnia again, irrespective of ethnic origin or religion. The witness's back garden overlooked the JNA garrison in Brcko town. The JNA training area was across the road from his workplace, and the garage facilities, about 200 metres away. From the end of 1990, the witness saw many JNA convoys passing through town. In 1991, he recalls seeing JNA weapons and equipment in Serb villages surrounding Brcko. In mid-1991, he saw the establishment of checkpoints manned by military policemen of the JNA and civilian policemen from Brcko municipality. He saw Serbs in Brcko being given weapons by the JNA. The witness recalls one occasion about a month before the conflict started in Brcko, when a JNA helicopter landed at the barracks in town and individuals wearing red berets got out. The witness continued to see helicopters landing at the barracks during the night. He saw men in camouflage uniform and red berets in the barracks premises almost every day, training soldiers, including the witness's Serb neighbours. He was later told by Rade Bozic that he was captain of a military police unit of the JNA for special purposes and that the Red Berets were members of those special units. Above him were Captain Dragan's soldiers from Serbia. The witness remembers two bridges being blown up in Brcko on the 30th of April, 1992. He later learned from Rade Bozic that he was responsible for blowing up both bridges. The witness says that the war broke out in Brcko on the 3rd of May, 1992. Between the 4th and 6th of May, he saw fighter aircraft in the Brcko area belonging to the JNA. They were flying low and soon after he would hear explosions in the Muslim/Croat majority part of town. The witness gives evidence about an ultimatum issued by members of the SDS party in Brcko, that the municipality should be split into three by the 4th of May, 1992. The witness saw this on television. On the 1st of May, Captain Petrovic, who introduced himself as the captain of the army unit in Brcko, of the military police force security, transmitted a message to the inhabitants of Brcko that his unit had been given the mandate to take over control of the town within 48 hours. On the 7th of May, Mr. Gasi witnessed the killing of civilians by men wearing camouflage uniforms and by civilian police in uniforms. On the 12th of May, he saw dead bodies in front of the Galeb Hotel in town. On one occasion, he saw bodies being unloaded into a hole dug out near to where his company was. The witness was arrested on the 27th of May, 1992. He was held in the SUP in Brcko and then taken to Luka camp. He was detained there from the 27th of May to the 7th of June,1992. He describes in his earlier testimony the camp conditions and personnel. Konstantin Simonovic, aka Kosta, described himself as the commander of Luka camp. The witness describes the physical abuse of detainees and an occasion when he witnessed the killing of at least two detainees. One of the perpetrators was one of the witness's Serb neighbours called Ranko Cesic. The witness describes another perpetrator who wore camouflage SMB uniform and was fond of introducing himself as a member of the Radical Party from Bijeljina, a Chetnik. He incised a cross onto the forehead of one detainee with a knife. Members of Arkan Tigers also came to the camp. The witness himself was beaten up by one of Arkan's men, who came to camp from time to time. The witness also testified about Goran Jelisic and his physical abuse of men at Luka camp. On one occasion, the witness describes that he had to take part in disposing of dead bodies at Luka camp into the River Sava. On one occasion, a vehicle pulled up at the camp. On it was written "The Republic Secretariat for the Interior of the Republic of Serbia." In it were a man in uniform, in camouflage, who was a major, and two civilian policemen, one wearing the insignia of the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia and one wearing the insignia of the Federal Ministry of the Interior. They came to see two men identified as Muslim sniper men. Both men, the witness describes, had been beaten regularly by Jelisic, one on questioning denied being a sniper. The major told Kosta to get both of them medical care. On the 7th of June, 1992, Rade Bozic came to Luka camp. He was accompanied by Kosta Simonovic. Bozic said he would do everything he could to get the witness out of the camp. He returned about two hours later and took the witness away. He drove the witness to a motel in Zvornik. When they arrived in front of the motel, the witness saw 30 or 40 Red Berets at the entrance. The witness met Captain Dragan. Bozic then drove the witness, Dragan, a woman from Dragan's fund, and a journalist to Belgrade. Dragan explained that the witness's wife and a sports friend from Belgrade had helped him and that was why he had been released from the camp. Your Honour, I have a few supplemental questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, during your first week at Luka camp, did there come a time when you were approached by a member of the camp personnel, who asked you a question about a phone number?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. A man walked up to me. I think he was a lieutenant colonel. He wore a reserve JNA uniform, and he asked me allegedly that first day -- or rather, the second day he -- I had already been questioned by a group of policemen. There were three of them in the office, and he said that he had listened to my interview and he heard that one of the questions was where my wife was, and I said that she was in Belgrade, staying with a friend. And then this --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Not lieutenant colonel, second lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I asked somebody to make a phone call to my wife and to tell her that I was still alive, and then I gave the number and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Did you later hear whether or not your wife had been contacted?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I found out about that later, when I was set free, when I was in Belgrade with this friend. Actually, he was the one who answered the telephone then, when that call was made. I mean, this friend, one of these Serbs. Now, I don't know whether it was exactly this one, but he's the only one who got the telephone number, and then he called this sports friend of mine and said that I was down there in Luka and that there were 48 hours -- or rather, they had 48 hours to get me out of Luka. That's what he told this friend of mine, and that they should go only to Captain Dragan, that he's the only one who could get me out of there, and if they did not get me out of there, then Ranko, one of these local men from Brcko, would come and that I'd get a bullet in my head.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Did your wife subsequently go to Dragan to ask for help?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I heard from my wife and from this sports friend of mine that this was in the early evening when this man who said he was a Serb and said that he called. The next morning they went to the Captain Dragan Foundation. She says it was around 7.00 in the morning. Well, I don't know exactly. But anyway, before anybody else would come. And then after a while -- I mean, she and this friend of mine were there and they were waiting in a hall. I mean, that's what she said to me. And she asked some people who worked there whether she could speak to Captain Dragan. However, then she told me later - and I heard about this from her and from that other friend of mine - it wasn't all that easy to see Captain Dragan, that he was not there and there was no chance for her to see him on that day. However, she was persistent. She stayed there and she stood there, I don't know for how long, and then all of a sudden she said that he got out of the elevator, this Captain Dragan, I guess, surrounded by, I don't know, say, four or five people wearing civilian uniforms. And then she jumped up. I guess she recognised him, because she had seen his picture in the newspaper somewhere. And then she got through all these people who were around him and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think we need the detail but we do need to understand what the story is. I mean, it appears to be -- is this it? Perhaps you can explain -- that the witness's wife was in Belgrade? Is this the point? She was told that she had to go and see Captain Dragan in order to get the witness out. Is this -- is this what he's trying to tell us? And then eventually she did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That's the point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's it. Yes. Yes. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Pause there, Mr. Gasi. You were subsequently picked up by Rade Bozic from Luka camp and taken away from there. Where did you go first with him?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: When he came to Luka, the first time he came I did not know why he had come, and that's what I said in my testimony earlier on. When I was walking out of that office, he asked me whether he could do something for me, and then I said, "Well, yes, get me out of here if I'm such a good man, as you had put it." And he said, "I'm going to see what I can do for you." And the second time he came he was accompanied by this man who did have a red beret on his head, and I think he was called Pedza, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Once he had picked you up from the camp, on the second occasion -- after the second occasion upon which he came there, where did he take you first in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: First I went to my apartment, accompanied by the two of them. I took my things from the apartment. And then he said to me, "Now you're going for a longish journey." He didn't tell me exactly where. He said: "You'll be set free, but you're going to take a longish journey." And then we set out from Brcko from the centre of town along the road to Bijeljina. We passed by my company -- or to be quite precise, we stopped at my company and the people there saw me, and then we went to Mistrafovica gasoline station and we turned right to the customs zone. When we got to the customs zone, then he parked the car right in front of the gate. Inside, within the parking lot --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Tell us, please, how long you remained at the customs zone.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Well, perhaps half an hour. I don't know exactly. Well, not more than half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what you saw there.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: In front of these buildings, there were vehicles that were parked. I think they were Pinzgauers, blue ones, and there were others too. What do they call them now in the JNA? Those combat vehicles for transporting the infantry. And it said, "Special Unit of the MUP of Serbia, Arkan's Tigers." That is what was written on this ordinary wooden board. And these vehicles were parked in front of these buildings. While he went over there -- I don't know. I saw him through the window. He talked to someone on the telephone, and then he came back and then he showed a finger to me, sort of thumbs up, this sign. And he said, "Everything is fine and we are going to go on from here."

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: These ordinary wooden boards that you describe, where were they positioned? You saw them at the customs zone; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, in front of these buildings where these vehicles were parked, they put those inscriptions on these wooden boards. I have no idea why this was done. Well, these vehicles were parked there anyway. I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. guess it was for the vehicles to park there. And later on, as we were driving, he said to me that the men from Serbia usually slept there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You then were driven to Zvornik. And I'm not going to ask you about the detail of that journey. We've already heard about that. During the course of that journey, you talked with Bozic. Did there come a time when he told you who he worked for? And who did he name?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. He asked whether I knew who stood behind my release. And I said, "I don't know." And he said, "Have you ever heard of Captain Dragan?" And I said, "Well, yes, I have, because I read about him sometime and he was on TV a few times when the war started in Croatia, saying that he was the commander of those Red Berets there, the Kninjas, as they were called, the Red Berets. And then this Captain Dragan was the reason why I would be set free. Apparently he was supposed to meet me and welcome me later on as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's an appropriate time. We'll adjourn now. Mr. Gasi, could you remember during this adjournment and any others there may be in your evidence not to speak to anybody about it until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. Thank you. We'll adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, these signs that you've described at the customs zone, can you tell us, please, were there other signs there, or were those the only signs that you saw?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I told you that there were blue Pinzgauers and there were these signs and there were also some combat vehicles. I think they belonged to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Mr. Gasi, were the signs you saw official signs or were they hand painted?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: What I told you I saw, they had signs written in colour and by hand to indicate where these various vehicles should be parked, and these boards were on the walls. For instance, members of the MUP of Serbia had a particular parking lot, then members of the Serbian Radical Party again, and I think there were Arkan's Tigers as well. Among others, there were APCs from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... next question: You drove in a car with Dragan to Belgrade. Tell us, please, what he said to you during that journey.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: For a while he was sitting in front, next to Rade Bozic. Then we had a break. I think it was in Muzice, at a motel there. Then he said he would come and sit by me on my right. And then he told me that I should come to his foundation once I had a bath, a shave, and everything, to write down on a couple of pages when I was arrested, who arrested me, all the things I had seen in Brcko before the war, when the war broke out, and all the things I had heard and seen at Luka, while I was imprisoned there; what kind of uniforms people wore when they came in, did anyone kill anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... can you tell us, please, did you subsequently go to Dragan's office and write something for him, as he had suggested you do?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I think it was two or three days later. Once I had put myself in order, I wrote down those two pages and took them to Captain Dragan's Fund.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Did you give him a full account of what had happened in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I don't know as to the full account. I did my best to write it down, to say I had seen Red Berets and various other people. I didn't mention them. I just said I saw people in camouflage uniform, people from the JNA, and some other things. But I didn't describe any specific killing or torture. I didn't say who the people were, what they looked like. When I gave it to him, he read it out and it was typed for him on two pages and then he called in someone -- called someone on the phone and told him that he should give him -- open the fax so -- he has something of interest to fax to him. I was sitting in the office, so I heard this. And then he dialled the number and faxed this to some other person, and we sat there for maybe half an hour --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: What happened after he --

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: -- talking about sport.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... did you receive a call after that?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: He called up again that same number and asked, "What do you think about all this?" And he indicated to me like this, indicating that I had done a good thing, that I was an okay guy, and that was all.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Pause there. That was a thumbs-up sign you indicated. Did he then -- what did he do with the fax after that?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: What I had written by hand and the typed version, he said to me, "You've done your bit, you're okay, you have no obligations towards me and you're free to go." And that was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gasi, first a question in reference to something you mentioned a moment ago, that there was a rally in Brcko attended by officials of the SDS and a minister from the government of Serbia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. I said that in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And this minister from Serbia was saying that everyone should live together.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: It wasn't an SDS rally. To be more accurate, it was the Prosvjeta Art and Culture Society that was holding a rally. And as I said in my testimony, almost everyone attended from the leadership of the Serbian Democratic Party. It was an open meeting held in the cultural centre, and everyone was speaking. There were a couple of academicians from Belgrade. Others were talking about tensions and things. Whereas, as far as I can remember, he was saying that no one had to write to separate by force the Serbian people in Bosnia from those in Serbia, that Serbia would always support the Serbian people in Bosnia. As for life together, to be quite frank, I can't remember. Maybe he may have said something to that effect. But this is what stuck in my memory. And of course, he was introduced -- I can't remember the name, but I think it was Cvjetinovic or Cvjetkovic or something like that. But that was along those lines that he spoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it wasn't really a rally. It was some kind of a cultural event by the culture and arts society, Prosvjeta.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. That is what it should have been. But it turned into more of a political rally. That is my opinion. Maybe -- I may be wrong, but that was the impression I had. And I didn't feel comfortable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When was this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but I think it was after the referendum in Bosnia and Herzegovina on independence. I think so. But please, I can't remember exactly the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, when a summary was read of your statement, I noted down that you said that this man said that everyone should live together.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I told you, and I repeat: If that is what was said, he may have said it. But I remember the part when he said that Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina should not worry, that Serbia would always stand with them. That is something that impressed me. He may have said other things, but this is what impressed me, and I am telling you that, to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's clear up one more thing. You were arrested on the 27th of May and released on the 7th of June; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So your testimony regarding those events relate to that ten-day period, because after ten days you left.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. Work it out. From the 27th of May to the 7th of June. I was arrested about 11.00 on the 27th of May and I was taken out on the 7th of June, around noon by Rade Bozic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This Rade Bozic that you mentioned, he was your neighbour?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: No, he's not my neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who is that man?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: In the testimony that you have probably received a copy of, it says that talking to him I learnt that he was a professional officer of the JNA. That is what he told me. And that he belongs to a special police special purpose unit. I think that he mentioned that he was born in Karlovac, in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And he was commander of the special unit of the military police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: That is what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Soldiers wearing red berets were in that unit.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Among others, he, too, had a red beret. He didn't put it on his head, but he had it folded on his shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You gave your statement to the investigators in April 1995. And at the very beginning you say that at the beginning you saw two JNA airplanes bombing a certain part of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Bombing a part of Brcko? I see them -- I saw them when they flew in from the south-easterly direction, and they were flying at a low altitude, and they passed by my building. And on the way back - I don't know how much later, a couple of minutes later - and as they returned, I heard explosions and detonations. Now, whether they bombed or not, I can't say. But anyway, once they had flown back past my building, explosions could be heard in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that this happened at the beginning of the fighting in Brcko; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean "At the beginning of the fighting in Brcko." This was the 2nd of May, I think, when I saw them. Now, whether the fighting started on the 2nd or the 4th or 5th of May in Brcko, I can't say with certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, I'm going to ask that you have a copy of your statement in front of you so you can refer to it when you want. Now, the accused's time is limited. He's only going to have about an hour to ask you questions, so could you for your part try and keep your answers as short as you can. Just concentrate on his questions, and if you can, answer them. If you can't understand them, just say so. Yes, Mr. Milosevic, your next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do my best to speed this up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who was fighting who in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was there in the north-western part of Brcko, which was allegedly bombed by these JNA planes? Did you see them actually bombing that part of Brcko?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I told you. I just heard explosions coming from that direction. Now, what they bombed, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether they bombed anything at all?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: They probably did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In this north-west section of Brcko, were there any significant strongholds of the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the investigators, you said that you were a member of the executive board of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From the 26th of May, 1990; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As a party activist and a member of the executive board, you were certainly familiar with the activities linked to the arming in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: No. I am not aware of that. I resigned just before the actual elections in Bosnia. As for arming, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In Copenhagen, you gave a statement on the 7th of May, 1993 to the Danish Helsinki Committee; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in it you said that there was shooting in the barricades in the Muslim parts of the town.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: What the Danish Helsinki Committee took from me, I was never given a copy in translation. I later received an English version. And what was stated in that interview was something that I didn't sign nor did I say that. They compiled this from statements from other people as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just pause a moment. Does the Prosecution have a copy?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In which language, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It's since been translated into B/C/S, so we have one in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, that's a copy of your statement, Mr. Gasi, and you can refer to it if you're asked my more questions about it. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that the greatest crimes were not committed by the army but paramilitary groups that arrived after the army. Does that concur with your own experience?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Let me tell you. I saw the Yugoslav army in town. Now, whether the army or I don't know who with the army committed the killings, I don't know. All I know is they had SMB uniforms in one colour and then camouflage uniforms. Now, you're referring again to this interview with the Danish Helsinki federation, which I don't abide by. What I do abide by is this other statement of which I signed every page. I did give an interview to this organisation through a very poor interpreter and I saw it for the first time when I came here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. In your statement, you mention the names of a certain number of local Serbs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which statement is that? Is this the one to the Prosecution or the Helsinki one?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Refer the witness to the passage.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are several names mentioned in many paragraphs. Throughout the statement he mentions various names. And that is why I'm trying to summarise this. On every page you can find a name that he mentions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you mean the policemen Ranko Cesic, Miso Cajevic, Dragan Zivkovic, Radivoje Knezevic, Stevo Knezevic, Dragan Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Goran Markovic, Pero -- from Brcko, Knezevic, Zivkovic, Cajevic, Cesic. Are they all locals from Brcko?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you link to these people something that happened in Brcko? As you say that people were killed, are these people responsible for those killings?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: One of them is. Ranko Cesic, I saw him kill two men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And did you see any JNA member killing someone?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I didn't see that. I didn't say I did in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking you, regardless of whether you said that or not. So you didn't see any JNA member killing anyone.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Well, Ranko Cesic, he belonged to the JNA. Who else could he have belonged to? He was wearing a camouflage uniform of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But these are people from Brcko that we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: He is from Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that on page 2, paragraphs 4 and 5, and page 3, paragraph 2, you link all those names to certain killings near Stari Grad? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: No. I'm not linking them. I didn't see them, because the people who were killing at Stari Grad, they had masks over their heads, hoods with openings for the eyes. So I didn't link them to that in my statement. I said they may have been, but not -- I did not accuse them in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 4, paragraph 1, you say that most of the soldiers you saw were from Bijeljina or Serbia. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Most of those who were guarding us, they introduced themselves. They said they -- where they were from. Those I had contact with were either from Bijeljina, Ugljevik, or villages around Bijeljina, those who wanted to talk to us. As for the one who beat me up on the first day, everyone told me that his name was Ivan, and I saw that he wore the patch of the Arkan's Tigers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't see anyone else from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Later on in my testimony you will find that, when these people came in a police Golf vehicle, and on the door was the emblem of the Republic of Serbia. They were members of the Ministry of the Interior, and this one major who entered inside accompanied by these two policemen, one of them wore the old Yugoslav coat of arms and the other one the emblem of the Republic of Serbia. They were policemen. And this JNA major was wearing a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see, a JNA major and two officers, one from the MUP of Serbia and one from the federal police. What did they want?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: They wanted to see Muslim snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were they some sort of investigators or something like that?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I don't know what they were. In any event, Kosta, who came with them, was asked to show them these two Muslim snipers. That is what they said out loud in the hangar, and then they came and saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Out of these that you mention as appearing there, listening to the summary, you said that the man in charge was Ranko Cesic, who was your neighbour; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I didn't say that he was in charge. I said that he came to Luka repeatedly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He's your neighbour?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, from my building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And there was someone from Bijeljina too.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Not just someone. There was -- on several occasions, there was Mirko Blagojevic; Vojvoda, the duke, who gave -- lectured us; then others who broke in at night and beat people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, those who came in the middle of the night and beat people, were they people from the area or were they people from Serbia or the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Camouflage uniforms, battery lamps, poles, telling us to sing about Serbian songs, about Arkan and Greater Serbia, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question is: Were they people from Serbia or the JNA or were they people that you knew, locals?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Those who were beating us that night, I don't know them. I have never seen them. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who is Mile Gatarevic, known as Bule?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: That's a local Serb from Brcko. Now, you're pulling that out of that Helsinki committee interview. I don't know how it got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't mention him?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: In this testimony for this Tribunal, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But in addition to that testimony, I also got a copy of this. I didn't make it up. I'm just asking you.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: He was a member of the Radical Party in Brcko, before the war, and he was in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did he commit a crime?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't see him in Luka while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you saw somebody being -- many people being killed from a house in the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: To be more precise, 14 or 15 were killed on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In this same statement, on page 3, paragraph 1, you saw that you saw 300 to 400 people being killed in a house from the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: That's a mistranslation. Again, the Helsinki committee put that, when they asked me what my assessment was of how many people were killed in Brcko in that period, I said 300 to 400. Now, how they placed that figure into this context, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did you see?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I said that I saw people being executed at Stari Grad. They shot a group of five or six; then at another spot, another five or six. And a policeman in a blue uniform killed three men, after turning them to face the wall, at close range.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who were those people who killed those civilians?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: One was in a blue police uniform. He had his back turned to me. Whereas, those who were killing on the road, who had lined people up against the wall, they were wearing SMB camouflage uniforms and they had black camouflage caps over their heads. And one of them, I heard, was shouting, "I want 30 for one of mine." That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I understood it that you were saying that there was a police chief by the name of Drago Veselic who was in command of that operation.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I did mention Drago Veselic, because they asked me at the Helsinki committee who the police chief was, and I told them. Now, how this came about, that you -- well, yes, he was actually a police chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, he wasn't linked up with the killings, was he, the ones you've just talked about?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Well, you could link him to them, because the SUP from the building is just 50 metres from the spot the killing took place, so I assume they heard the killing take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, on the 27th of May, 1992 on the premises of Elektrobrcko you were arrested by two policemen; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were they policemen whom you knew from Brcko?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I knew both of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you saw a police inspector. Was he from Brcko too?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Which police inspector? These two policemen took me to the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that's when you saw the police inspector in the building?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: No, they came to Luka. The police inspectors came to Luka, not on that first day but on the second day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say that a certain man named Pero transferred you to the hangars in Luka where you were met by a certain man called Miodrag Nedic.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Pudic met me and he was a policeman before the war, and I think he's still a policeman actually. So he was there and he wanted to take a pistol to hit me on the head with it. But he changed his mind and took me into an office. Now, why they took me there, I don't know. But there was a lieutenant colonel sitting there and two other men on his right. One of them had a cockade on his uniform, a big beard too, and he jumped up and was going to hit me on the head with the nozzle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that at that time or even before that actual period of time, JNA units were not there at all?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: What do you mean weren't there? I saw them on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What JNA unit did you see? Who did you see belonging to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: In Brcko itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Everyone from the barracks and opposite the training ground belonging to my own company, all of them were there. And on one occasion Colonel Milinkovic came -- Lieutenant Colonel Milinkovic came with an escort. They came to my company's building and I saw them at the gates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, on page 6, paragraph 5 of your statement, you say that three or four local Serbs wearing police uniforms asked for volunteers from amongst the prisoners in order to clean the SUP building up. And then you go on to say that amongst them you recognised Pero and Miso Cajevic, also people whom you happened to know from Brcko; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: You seem to be referring to the Helsinki committee again. All right. But yes, Pero was with them and so was Miso Cajevic. And I didn't put myself forward as a volunteer. Another one wearing a camouflage uniform said, "Come on, you. You've got a lot of muscle. You go and do the job."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then when you were at the SUP building itself, you saw the killing of two of the prisoners there from Luka; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where did this actually take place?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: In the SUP building by the garages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean in the yard of the building, then?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who did the killings?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I told you, I didn't recognise the men. One of the men was shot straight away in the parking lot. The other one escaped and started to flee and then this other man took up an automatic rifle and shot at him in his -- at his feet, but then he came up close to him and killed him from short range. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were these the local policemen too? Because you said you saw three policemen wearing summer police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I don't know. I couldn't see from where I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Were these the two detainees -- you saw two detainees being killed, you said, at the camp. Are these two at the SUP building those two, or did you see other people being killed at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They took us out of Luka. There were about 10 to 15 of us in the group. Now, whether they killed two men from that particular group, I can't tell you, because there were other people in the SUP building. But there was a general noise and commotion, and when that happened, I heard people rush up the stairs and say, "Where are the others? Kill the others too." That's what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did you -- just one moment, Mr. Milosevic. There's something I want to clarify. Did you see anybody being killed at the camp itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I saw Ranko Cesic take four men out of the office, and I saw him hit two of them, who fell to the ground. Now, whether they were shot down dead, I don't know. But he shot from a distance of 2 metres in -- at their backs. They were hit. They fell to the ground. Now, whether they were dead or not, I can't say. And that happened in Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And how many men do you know or can you give us some idea how many men were in the Luka camp at the time that you were? Do you have any idea or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did count the men at one time, and there were between 150 and 200 of them, depending. They would come and go. Sometimes they would go and not come back, and I don't know what happened to them. So there was between 120 to 200.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And before the war, what had the camp been? What was it? Was it a camp before the war or was it something else? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was Luka, a port, and the ships would bring in their cargo. It was actually a port, Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Well, just one further thing: Do you know how many men were killed in all in Luka? Maybe you don't. But if you do, perhaps you could tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my statement, I said that I saw those two men being killed by Ranko Cesic. Now, I don't know how many more there were. On one occasion, when we were throwing the corpses into the port, I would say that -- now, whether these people were killed in the port or brought in from elsewhere, but on that heap of bodies I think there were about 20 of them, plus the two that I saw being -- were killed. I don't know whether that is the total number or not, but that's what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But you said in paragraph 1 on page 7 of your statement - and you refer to that statement - you said: "I watched the incident for about two minutes. I didn't know the victims. However, I do know that they were from Brcko. We were afraid after the shooting, and after the shooting in the office from which we watched the shootings, Boro Kaurinovic turned up, a police officer before the fighting began, and he told us to stay in the office." Now, this policeman, he told you to remain in the office to prevent you from getting hurt; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Well, he pushed us into another office. And what you asked me about a moment ago about the two men who were killed, I heard about that from others, so I assumed that they were from Brcko, but I didn't actually know them myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But this man Boro Kaurinovic, who was also from Brcko, as you say, did he actually save your life? Because he took you off and pushed you into another building and stopped you from getting hurt.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, probably that was it. The one that did the shouting outside asked, "Where are the other Turks so we can kill them too?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there was general chaos there, was there, and this Boro Kaurinovic, who was an inhabitant of your town set you aside in another office to prevent the others from killing you and then you were returned to Luka, the port; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Well, as to the general chaos, I wouldn't put it that way, because everything was nonetheless controlled by the JNA. I think that everything was controlled from the garrison by them there. So yes, they did sort of save -- well, perhaps that man did save me at that particular point in time, and I thank him for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In paragraph 2 on page 8, you speak of the killing of four detainees from Luka, when, as you say, you recognised Ranko Cesic, a man called Miso Cajevic, and another man whom we mentioned previously, Pudic -- or you mentioned Pudic.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. Pudic was always there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, all these three men that I -- whose names I've just read out, were they the people from Brcko?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. You've just mentioned some 20 corpses that you happened to notice in a part of the hangar, and among those bodies you recognised that of Sead Cerimagic and of Elvedin Salkanovic. Now, do you know who killed those people?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: You said in a part of the hangar. It wasn't a part of the hangar. They took us out to the banks of the River Sava, behind the hangar, actually, and that's where this heap of corpses was. As to recognising these people, well, I saw the T-shirt that one of the guys were wearing and he was also a member of our sports club and he would wear that kind of T-shirt, so I assume that was him, one of them was him. As to the others, as to Sead's killing, I really can't be sure whether I actually recognised him. Perhaps I did. Anyway, it was difficult to recognise anybody; only if you remembered some detail as to what they were wearing, their clothing or anything of that kind. Otherwise, all those were corpses. It was actually very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. On page 10, paragraph 2, you go on to say that you and the other detainees in Luka knew that the commander of the camp was a man called Vojkan Djurkovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Major Djurkovic. He came two or three times. He came into the hangar. And then the detainees would gather round him, and he would give a speech of some kind and tell us how he saved somebody's life, and he'd say, "I saved your brother's life," and he would address a detainee. And he said that he was the camp commander to begin with. Now, I don't know whether he actually was or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was he a major of the army of Republika Srpska and also a local inhabitant?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I don't know of him being a major of the army of Republika Srpska. The only army that existed was the JNA in Brcko. Now, what it came to be called later on, I really can't say. I think he said that he was a native of Bijeljina, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, all right. That's the same region, isn't it, the same general area.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Well, Brcko, Bijeljina, maybe it is. It's at a distance of some 50 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, all right. But do you know that he actually ordered any killing? Because I can see from what you say here that the detainees said he was good to them and that his men would bring them cigarettes and things like that.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Well, I didn't describe what he brought in or didn't, but from what I heard, at the time the killings took place mostly at the beginning, when the camp -- Luka camp first opened. Now, who brought whom cigarettes and whether anybody brought cigarettes in at all, I don't know. I am not a smoker myself so I wasn't interested in that, so I really can't say. I don't know. All I do know is that I was beaten black and blue by them while I was there and so were others. Others were beaten too. And that's it. Now, whether they came to bring in cigarettes or anything of the kind, or took people off to clean their cars, wash their cars and then they would be brought back, and things like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned the name of a Chetnik named Enver; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if his name was Enver, I assume he was a Muslim, wasn't he, and I also assume it must have been a local inhabitant, a local of some kind.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: He had patches on which denoted a Chetnik, with the cockade. And he said his name was Enver and that he was a Chetnik; that is to say, a member of the Radical Party too. Now, whether he gave us his real name or not, I can't say. I don't know people and I can't recognise ethnic groups judging by the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if he was -- his name was Enver, he couldn't have been a Serb.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Well, I can say my name is George and I wouldn't be an American.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So ten days later, on the 7th of June, when you were released, you were released by this man called Rade Bozic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, on the 7th of June. Right. The 7th of June. Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And he told you that he was a Serb from Karlovac in Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: He said that he was a professional captain of the military police and that he was born in Karlovac in Croatia. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then on page 11, paragraph 3, you say that Rade Bozic said that he was a professional soldier of the JNA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that was the only member of the JNA whom you mention as being a direct participant in any of the events you discuss in your statements; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Well, it's not quite right, because when I went outside, I saw tanks and transporters, APCs lined up. And when I moved around town, I saw JNA checkpoints manned by the police, manned by people wearing red berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't understand me, Mr. Gasi. I said that that was the only member of the JNA whom you mention as being a direct participant in the events, whose name you give us. That's the only man, isn't it, the one who took you out of the camp.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: He took me out of the camp. Nobody else took me out; he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he took you out and took you away from Brcko to Zvornik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that's where you got to know Captain Dragan. You met Captain Dragan; right?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were freed at the initiative of Captain Dragan who -- and your wife asked him to do her that favour; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you were taken out of Luka by this man Rade Bozic.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At his intervention --

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, that's what he said. He said the big boss had ordered him to take me to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And then he told you that while you were on your way to Belgrade together, that you should rest up for a few days, as you say on page 7, paragraph 1 of your statement, to have a rest for four days, have a rest for four days and write down everything you experienced and saw; is that it?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then he typed out that statement of yours, or somebody typed it out for him, and he faxed it to someone, did he?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know who he sent the fax to?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, is it true, then, that that sending out of your report or statement was his attempt to record your experience and stay in Luka camp as testimony to what happened there, to gather information about what was going on there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness can't tell us what Captain Dragan was thinking unless he -- Did he tell you, Mr. Gasi, why he was asking you to make this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I told you before. He said, "Sit down, have a rest, and write everything you saw before the war in Brcko, everything you saw during the war in Brcko, and everything you saw while you were in Luka at Brcko, what types of uniforms you saw," and that's what I did. I wrote all that down for him. Now, I don't know who he sent it to or why he sent it to anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He didn't tell you why he wanted you to write all this down; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he didn't. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, you asked him to help your brothers. And according to what you had learnt, they were in the Batkovic camp as detainees; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: His answer to you was that he couldn't help you on that score.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: The first time he didn't give me an answer, so I had to go again, and he said he'd see what he could do. But I never heard anything from him after that. So he said, "Don't contact me. Don't call me. I'll call you via friends and let you know," but I don't know what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, does that mean that when you were freed he pulled some strings of his, personal ones, and used his authority, which he wasn't able to use anywhere else, so he wielded that authority and used his personal connections, did he?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know. I can't say what connections he had and what his relationship was. But Rade said it was the big boss who was letting me go, that's all. Now, whether he wanted to free anybody else, I don't know, or whether he could have, I don't know. All I know is that I was freed at his initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But this lieutenant colonel who asked for your wife's telephone number to be able to tell her where you were, this second lieutenant, he just said that this man could help you; is that it?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: He told my wife and that friend of mine that it was only Captain Dragan who would be able to pull me out of there. That's what he said. And that's what I heard from my wife and from the man who was with my wife. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So he assumed that he knew somebody. He had some connections. There were no organs from Serbia who would be able to intervene in your behalf.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In your statement given to the investigators, on page 8, paragraph 3, you quote the names of 13 individuals and then a further 13, and of these you say that you don't believe they're still alive, that they survived. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: When I gave the statement to the Helsinki Committee, they asked me whether I remembered all the people who were with me. Now, I do know a lot of people from Brcko by sight, so I gave the names of the people whom I assumed -- actually, most of these people from the list have disappeared. Other detainees said that they were in Luka. Others on the list have remained, those names which I remember. So actually, I would like to have been able to remember all 200 names, but I'm afraid I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So how, then, did you assume that these other 13 were not alive? Do you have any reason and grounds for saying that?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I've just said. The people on that list -- the list was drawn up by the Helsinki Committee, and it was on the basis of what I had heard. Now, what I saw and what I knew about I state in the statement signed by me, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But are you the author of a letter addressed to the Bosnian newspaper Ljiljan and the public at large?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: No, I'm not. That was a journalist from Brcko. He's a friend of mine. And he is one of the people who wrote the letter, and I added something. But I don't think it was ever published.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And was that your personal reaction? It was written in June 1994. It was a television programme, Tamo Daleko, broadcast by Radio BH; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Well, yes, it was a radio programme, a radio broadcast, and we did listen to it while we were in Denmark, at the centre there. And this journalist -- we grew up together, actually, so he did interviews with me. But I think that he was incarcerated in the Partizan and that he was -- he died. So he was the person who wrote that. Now, there are some things that I told him about, but most of the things in the letter are his, so I don't want to enter into whether they are correct or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, is it true that the role of the JNA and the Brcko garrison was realistically portrayed in the radio broadcasts?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Well, I can't say, because the man who did them -- I'm not sure. I can't tell you for sure. I'm not 100 per cent certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. This letter of yours, does it represent a criticism of the local Muslim leadership by and large and not a testimony of any crimes perpetrated by JNA members?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Well, the local Muslim leadership, you say? Well, all of that -- let me tell you again that I'm not the person who wrote the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was compiled as the result of talks you had with that journalist; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm not the author. That's not my style to write letters like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Could the witness have a copy of this letter if there are going to be many more questions on it. We do have a copy of it in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness see it. Mr. Milosevic, time is short. Have you got very much more for this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would actually like to finish with this witness now, because obviously there is no additional information that he can provide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. If you would be as quick as you can. There are some additional matters -- administrative matters, I understand, the Prosecution want to raise. We'll try and do all that before quarter to. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May. I should like to thank the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gasi, you gave your statement to the investigators in 1995. This statement that was referred to a while ago, and this is the statement that was given in Denmark on the 7th of May, 1993 at the Danish-Helsinki committee in Copenhagen. That's where you gave this statement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In this statement of yours dated the 4th and 5th of April, 1995, everything you said about the Yugoslav army is contained in paragraph 3, where you mentioned those aircraft. In that statement of yours, there are two more places where you mention, in one case Slobodan Mitric, a former reserve captain of the JNA, and in another place you mention also a former JNA captain. Throughout this statement, you do not mention a single action that was taken by the JNA, absolutely nothing, except for this which has to do with the aircraft that were allegedly doing the bombing. How do you explain that, that in your statement there is no reference to the JNA distributing weapons, that you saw those helicopters delivering the Red Berets, nothing? There is no mention of that in your first statement. Everything that you said in your first statement only had to do with the bombing. Can you explain that to the Judges, please.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I gave this statement for this court and I signed each and every page. Had you asked me about it today, I would have talked to you about it today. At the Helsinki committee --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not asking you about the Helsinki committee. I'm asking you about what you said to the investigators. You did not tell the investigators anything about actions of the JNA, except for those two aircraft.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: What do you mean I didn't? Then you got the wrong report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the Office of the Prosecutor is there, and they will probably react if I do something that is impermissible. I heard you full well, that you said that at one point in time the aircraft were bombing an area in Brcko that was populated predominantly by Bosniaks and Croats. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In that part of town, were there also some Serb inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Well, if you want, 90 per cent of the population of that part of Brcko are Muslims and Croats. But there are some Serbs too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Bombs cannot select their victims.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. You've given your explanation. However, when you spoke to the Helsinki committee, you said that you did trust the federal army and you did not object in any way to the behaviour of the JNA at the time.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: How can a man who grew up in Yugoslavia not trust the JNA? But then when they disappoint you, then you lose all that faith and trust, everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I have to hurry up. Unfortunately, I have read your statement that you gave to the investigators and you talked about individual incidents there and each and every human life is precious and you saw several civilians being killed at certain points in time. However, here before the Helsinki committee you said the following. I would like to put all of this to you. Some of it had already been put to you. You were in the centre of town, and from the apartment where you were, you saw a few of these killings with your very own eyes.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But here you said before the Helsinki committee: "In the house, in the centre of town, Gasi saw from the house that 300 to 400 persons were killed. Some were kept in a bunker that had previously been --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He has been asked this, Mr. Tapuskovic. He's given his explanation. So I think we have the point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Your Honour Judge May, that is not what was mentioned. He said from the bunker they had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We really have got time against us. Now, he's been thoroughly cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic. I know you're the friend of the court. What we might do is this: We don't at the moment have the Helsinki statement. Would you suggest -- would you suggest that we have that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do suggest that you should have that, and I'm about to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: He said that from that bunker he saw groups of 30 to 40 men being taken out and executed and that for days blood was washed off the square. This is something compiled by the Helsinki committee and they probably used that as an important document later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. What is it you want to ask the witness about that?
