utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why didn't he tell the investigators about all these things? After all, Your Honours, I would like to conclude by saying the following: In respect of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him answer. Yes, you can briefly deal with that, Mr. Gasi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I answered Mr. Milosevic. You should have listened. The Helsinki committee, when they asked me about my estimate as to how many people were killed in Brcko at the beginning of May and June, I said 300 to 400. That's what I said in that statement that you've mentioned just now. I remember this very well. They asked me and I remember what I said to them. I remember that very well. Now, what they wrote down, I don't know about that. They asked me, "What do you think? Where were they bringing these people from?" Underneath the old town there is an atomic shelter, Mr. Tapuskovic. And as I heard later in Luka, many people were detained there. Now, were they bringing them from there? That's something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to conclude by asking you did you actually see 30 or 40 men being executed in this way, by firing squad?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI
utterances.text: I said to Mr. Milosevic that then, when I was watching, between 14 to 15 people were killed at the most. That was the maximum.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Pack, if you can deal with any re-examination you have briefly, because time is against us.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: No re-examination. Just a couple of matters to assist Your Honours. You've been handed a document headed "The Danish Helsinki Committee." I don't know what Mr. Tapuskovic was getting at insofar as the JNA references were concerned. But I could perhaps point out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but he was talking about the Prosecution statement --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- apparently in that connection.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, in that case, I shan't point out anything from that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We better give this Helsinki document a C number, a court number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a couple of matters to assist the Chamber and the accused and amici. Because the testimony this week has taken longer than forecast, we will not now be calling one of the 92 bis witnesses next week. Whether we call him later on or not, I'm not sure. But we certainly won't be calling him next week, so that there is no need to prepare Witness B-1524, who in the printed list would follow van Linden. So far as van Linden is concern, as I am at present advised he is available for Monday and not Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. beyond. I'm pressing for information about limitations on his travel, but it may be that he has commitments elsewhere that he can't get out of for Tuesday. And accordingly, there is a possibility that we will be asking for him to be taken on Monday come what may. I know it's desirable, but I thought it better to mention it now rather than later. Can I mention something in private session for 30 seconds, to help?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I am doing everything I can, obviously, to prepare for the final list of witnesses that it's possible for us to call in the available time. There's a couple of motions coming your way soon, one dealing with one of the hitherto unnamed witnesses to deal with intercepts. And it will obviously assist us if that motion can be dealt with quickly. And there will be a composite motion that will so far as possible deal with all outstanding witness lists and witness matters between now and the end of the case. We've been reviewing the witness list, and I think I'm going to be in a position very soon to identify a number of witnesses whom it would not be worthwhile preparing, because I don't think we're going to be able to fit them in, and so I'll provide that list, I hope, if not by tomorrow, by Monday, to help the accused, the amicus, Chamber, and the accused's associates. Finally, I have some maps. At the moment enough for the Chamber and for the accused. One for the amicus will follow later. The Chamber will recall that we provided maps at an earlier stage when there -- it happened to be at the time when there was a change in the Rules about the Chamber's powers to rule on sufficiency of crime-base evidence. And the maps showed what had been -- what the Prosecution say had been proved fully or incompletely or not at all in various areas of Croatia and Bosnia by reference to what it was originally intended to prove in the indictment. A similar matter but to a slightly different effect was produced for Bosnia; Bosnia, of course, being very much a work in progress. There are three maps here for Kosovo. They do the same thing, but they're broken down according to three topics: deportation, killing sites, sexual abuse and cultural monuments. And they again show by reference to counts in the indictment what the Prosecution believes it has proved in full or -- has called all the evidence of. Whether it's proved it or not is another matter. It's called all the evidence on particular topics or it's called no evidence or it's called some of the evidence. I hope that will be helpful. I think it was originally the Chamber that thought these might be of value to them. And that's one for the accused. And Mr. Tapuskovic's copy will be available later today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Judges' copies will be kept in the court and can be handed in later. Is there anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, I don't think so, Your Honour. I shan't be here tomorrow, but I will be here on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll adjourn now until 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 1.50 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 12th day of September, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.
